smt-2023-geometry-01.title: Compare side lengths
smt-2023-geometry-01.body:
Let $A_1A_2=1$. Each interior angle of the dodecagon is $150^\circ$.

At $A_2$: $\angle B_1A_2B_2=360^\circ-150^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=90^\circ$ with $A_2B_1=A_2B_2=1$, so $B_1B_2=\sqrt2$.

At $A_2$: $\angle C_1A_2C_2=150^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$ with $A_2C_1=A_2C_2=1$, so $C_1C_2=\sqrt{2-2\cos30^\circ}=\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt2}$.

Both new dodecagons are regular, so the area ratio is the square of the side ratio: $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{(\sqrt3-1)/\sqrt2}\right)^2=\frac{4}{(\sqrt3-1)^2}=\frac{4}{4-2\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{2-\sqrt3}=4+2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $4+2\sqrt3$**

smt-2023-geometry-02.title: Difference of two cones
smt-2023-geometry-02.body:
Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ onto line $BC$. Angle $C$ is obtuse, so $D$ lies beyond $C$ on ray $BC$. Let $CD=x$, $AD=y$: $(x+16)^2+y^2=39^2$ and $x^2+y^2=25^2$. Subtracting gives $32x+256=39^2-25^2=896$, so $x=20$, and $y=\sqrt{625-400}=15$.

The solid is the cone from rotating $\triangle ABD$ with the cone from rotating $\triangle ACD$ removed. Both have radius $15$; the heights are $BD=36$ and $CD=20$. Volume $=\frac13\pi\cdot15^2\cdot(36-20)=\frac13\pi\cdot225\cdot16=1200\pi$.

**Answer: $1200\pi$**

smt-2023-geometry-03.title: Similar figures with ratio $\frac13$
smt-2023-geometry-03.body:
The inradius of $\triangle ABC$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, so $\Omega_0$ has area $\frac{4\pi}{3}$.

Consider the chain at vertex $A$. The triangle has height $2\sqrt3$, and $\Omega_0$ touches $\Omega_{1A}$ at the top of $\Omega_0$, which is at distance $\frac{4\sqrt3}{3}-\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}=\frac13\cdot2\sqrt3$ from $A$. The common tangent there is parallel to $BC$ and cuts off a small equilateral triangle at $A$, similar to $\triangle ABC$ with ratio $\frac13$, whose incircle is $\Omega_{1A}$. The same picture repeats inside it, so each circle in the chain is $\frac13$ the radius, i.e. $\frac19$ the area, of the previous one.

The circles at vertex $A$ have areas $\frac{4\pi}3\left(\frac19\right)^i$ for $i\ge1$, total $\frac{4\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{1/9}{1-1/9}=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

Total $=\frac{4\pi}3+3\cdot\frac\pi6=\frac{11\pi}6$.

**Answer: $\frac{11\pi}{6}$**

smt-2023-geometry-04.title: Pythagorean relations
smt-2023-geometry-04.body:
Let $O_1$ be the center of $\Omega$, $O_2$ the center of $\omega$, $O_3$ and $r$ the center and radius of the desired circle $\omega'$. In the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle $O_1BM$, $O_1M=\frac12$, so $MD=1-\frac12=\frac12$ and $\omega$ has radius $\frac14$.

Measure heights above $BC$ along line $MD$ (perpendicular to $BC$ at $M$): $O_2$ is at height $\frac14$, $O_1$ at height $-\frac12$, and $O_3$ at height $r$ (the circle is tangent to $BC$). Let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O_3$ to line $MD$, at height $r$. Then $O_2E=\left|\frac14-r\right|$ and $O_2O_3=\frac14+r$, so $O_3E=\sqrt{\left(\frac14+r\right)^2-\left(\frac14-r\right)^2}=\sqrt r$.

In right triangle $O_1O_3E$: $O_1O_3=1-r$, $O_1E=\frac12+r$, so $r+\left(\frac12+r\right)^2=(1-r)^2$, i.e. $r+\frac14+r+r^2=1-2r+r^2$, so $4r=\frac34$ and $r=\frac3{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3}{16}$**

smt-2023-geometry-05.title: Area of each pentagon
smt-2023-geometry-05.body:
The distance from $O$ to a side of $\triangle ABC$ is $2\sqrt3$. The pentagon between $OA_3$ and $OB_3$ splits into $\triangle OA_3A_2$, $\triangle OA_2B_1$, $\triangle OB_1B_3$. The segment $A_3A_2$ has length $\frac a2$ and its distance from $O$ is $4\sqrt3-\frac{a\sqrt3}{2}$; similarly for the third triangle; and $A_2B_1=12-a-b$ is at distance $2\sqrt3$. The pentagon area is

$\frac12\cdot\frac a2\left(4\sqrt3-\frac{a\sqrt3}2\right)+\frac12\cdot2\sqrt3(12-a-b)+\frac12\cdot\frac b2\left(4\sqrt3-\frac{b\sqrt3}2\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}8(96-a^2-b^2)$.

Similarly for the other two. The cut-out triangles have total area $\frac{\sqrt3}4(a^2+b^2+c^2)=18\sqrt3$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2=72$.

The three pentagon quantities sum to $288-2\cdot72=144$, so in ratio $5:6:7$ they are $40,48,56$. Hence $a^2+b^2,\,b^2+c^2,\,c^2+a^2$ are $56,48,40$ in some order, giving $\{a^2,b^2,c^2\}=\{16,24,32\}$, i.e. $\{a,b,c\}=\{4,2\sqrt6,4\sqrt2\}$ (all less than $6$).

$abc=4\cdot2\sqrt6\cdot4\sqrt2=32\sqrt{12}=64\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $64\sqrt3$**

smt-2023-geometry-06.title: Excircle and a similarity ratio
smt-2023-geometry-06.body:
$\omega_2$ is the $A$-excircle of $\triangle AFG$, so $AX=AY=s$, the semiperimeter of $\triangle AFG$. Let $a=FG$ and $s=ka$; the condition $4s=5a$ gives $k=\frac54$.

The $A$-exradius of $\triangle AFG$ is $\frac{[AFG]}{s-a}=\frac{rs}{s-a}=\frac{k}{k-1}r$ where $r$ is the inradius of $\triangle AFG$. Since $\omega_2$ is the incircle of $\triangle ADE$, $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle AFG$ with ratio $\frac{k}{k-1}=5$. The same argument one level up gives that the inradius of $\triangle ABC$ (radius of $\omega_1$) is $\left(\frac k{k-1}\right)^2r=25r$.

So $r=\frac{60}{25}$ and the radius of $\omega_2$ is $5r=\frac{60}5=12$.

**Answer: 12**

smt-2023-geometry-07.title: Angle bisector and triple-angle formulas
smt-2023-geometry-07.body:
Let $\angle BAC=3\alpha$ and $AB=x$. In $\triangle ADC$, $AE$ bisects $\angle DAC$, so $\frac{AD}{AC}=\frac{DE}{EC}=\frac35$ and $AD=3$. Then $\triangle ADC$ has sides $3,4,5$ (with $DC=4$), so $\angle ADC=90^\circ$.

Since $AD$ bisects $\angle BAE$ and is perpendicular to $BE$, triangle $BAE$ is isosceles with $AE=AB=x$.

Then $BF=x\sin3\alpha$, $AF=x\cos3\alpha$, $EG=x\sin\alpha$, $AG=x\cos\alpha$. Because $BF\parallel EG$, $\frac{CF}{CG}=\frac{BF}{EG}=\frac{\sin3\alpha}{\sin\alpha}=3-4\sin^2\alpha$, and $\frac{AF}{AG}=\frac{\cos3\alpha}{\cos\alpha}=4\cos^2\alpha-3$.

Hence the difference is $3-4\sin^2\alpha-4\cos^2\alpha+3=6-4=2$.

**Answer: 2**

smt-2023-geometry-08.title: Similar triangles and Ptolemy
smt-2023-geometry-08.body:
Since $R$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, $RA=RC$, so $\angle RCA=\angle RAC=\angle CAB$ and hence $RC\parallel AB$. Thus $\triangle AQB\sim\triangle CQR$ and $QC=\frac{RC}{AB}\cdot AQ=\frac{RC}{3}$ (as $AB=6$).

Let $AR=RC=x$. Then $AC=2+\frac x3$. In the cyclic quadrilateral $ARCP$ with $RC\parallel AP$, it is an isosceles trapezoid, so $PC=AR=x$ and $PR=AC=2+\frac x3$.

Ptolemy: $AP\cdot RC+AR\cdot PC=AC\cdot PR$, i.e. $x+x^2=\left(2+\frac x3\right)^2$. This simplifies to $8x^2-3x-36=0$, with positive root $x=\frac{3+\sqrt{1161}}{16}=\frac{3+3\sqrt{129}}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3+3\sqrt{129}}{16}$**

smt-2023-geometry-09.title: Radical axis
smt-2023-geometry-09.body:
The excircle opposite $B$ touches lines $BA,BC$ at points at distance $\frac{P_{ABC}}2$ from $B$. Since $BP=BQ=\frac{P_{ABC}}4$, $P$ and $Q$ are the midpoints of those tangent segments. So $P$ and $Q$ have equal power with respect to $\odot I_B$ and to the point-circle $B$: the power of $P$ is $\left(\frac{P_{ABC}}{4}\right)^2$ in both cases. Hence line $PQ$ is the radical axis of $\odot I_B$ and $B$, so for $S$ on $PQ$, $ST^2=SB^2$ and $ST=SB$.

Now $AC=AB=\frac1{2\sin18^\circ}=\frac{1}{(\sqrt5-1)/2}=\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}$, so $P_{ABC}=1+(\sqrt5+1)=\sqrt5+2$ and $BP=BQ=\frac{\sqrt5+2}4$.

The excenter $I_B$ lies on the internal bisector of $\angle ABC=72^\circ$. Triangle $BPQ$ is isosceles ($BP=BQ$), so this bisector meets $PQ$ at its midpoint $S$ with $BS\perp PQ$ and $\angle PBS=36^\circ$. Therefore $BS=BP\cos36^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5+2}4\cdot\frac{\sqrt5+1}4=\frac{7+3\sqrt5}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{7+3\sqrt5}{16}$**

smt-2023-geometry-10.title: Central angles
smt-2023-geometry-10.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcenter (inside the triangle, which is acute) and $R=\frac{13\cdot14\cdot15}{4\cdot84}=\frac{65}8$. The bisector from $C$ meets the circle at the midpoint $F$ of arc $AB$, so $\angle AOF=\angle FOB=C$ (twice the inscribed angle $\frac C2$). Likewise $\angle BOD=\angle DOC=A$ and $\angle COE=\angle EOA=B$.

The hexagon splits into six triangles at $O$, each with two sides $R$:

$[AFBDCE]=\frac12R^2(2\sin A+2\sin B+2\sin C)=R^2(\sin A+\sin B+\sin C)$.

By the Law of Sines $\sin A=\frac{BC}{2R}$ etc., so this equals $R\cdot\frac{AB+BC+CA}{2}=R\cdot s=\frac{65}8\cdot21=\frac{1365}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{1365}8$**

smt-2023-geometry-10.title: Add three isosceles triangles to $\triangle ABC$
smt-2023-geometry-10.body:
The hexagon is $[ABC]+[DBC]+[ECA]+[FAB]$, with $[ABC]=84$. Triangle $DBC$ is isosceles with legs $2R\sin\frac A2$ and apex angle $180^\circ-A$, so $[DBC]=R^2(1-\cos A)\sin A$; similarly for the others. With $\sin A=\frac{56}{65},\cos A=\frac{33}{65}$, $\sin B=\frac{12}{13},\cos B=\frac5{13}$, $\sin C=\frac45,\cos C=\frac35$ this gives

$84+\frac{4225}{64}\left(\frac{32}{65}\cdot\frac{56}{65}+\frac8{13}\cdot\frac{12}{13}+\frac25\cdot\frac45\right)=84+28+37.5+21.125=\frac{1365}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{1365}8$**
